card: Paper card. Question: Which deconvolution-based peak profile analysis methods (conventional vs. modified) best characterize the dislocation structure and crystallite size of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy during plastic deformation, and how do these structural parameters evolve with strain?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase FCC). Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (12 remelts, flipped every 2nd melt) to form ~30g ingots; wire discharge machining into cylinders (5 mm diameter, 8 mm height); axial compression at room temperature with a strain rate of ~8.4·10−3 s−1 to engineering strains of 0.00, 25.00, 37.50, 42.50, 47.50, and 55.00%. Test conditions: Synchrotron X-ray diffraction (transmission mode, beamline 5-A, VEPP-4) using 50.12 keV photons (0.0247 nm wavelength); microhardness tests (HV0.1) on deformed specimens. Findings: The conventional Williamson-Hall (cWH) method shows poor correlation with experimental data, with adjusted R² values ranging from 0.1 to 0.5.; Correcting for elastic modulus (WHEhkl method) significantly reduces approximation error compared to cWH.; The modified Williamson-Hall (mWH) method provides the best fit, yielding R² values above 0.8.; Dislocation density increases with strain and reaches a plateau at an engineering strain of 47.5%.; The average dislocation density at the plateau is approximately 40·10¹⁴ m⁻².; Crystallite size (CSR) decreases with strain up to 41.5–47.5% and remains constant thereafter.; Microhardness increases significantly up to 42.5% strain but shows little change at higher strains.; The Wilkens parameter (M) increases continuously, indicating a disordered dislocation structure rather than a cell structure.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the failure of conventional methods to the elastic anisotropy and intrinsically high lattice distortion of the HEA. They argue that the modified methods (mWH/mWA) succeed by incorporating a dislocation model of strain anisotropy and contrast factors. The saturation of dislocation density at 47.5% strain is explained by the classical concept where nucleation and annihilation rates of dislocations become equal. The continuous increase in the Wilkens parameter suggests the dislocation structure becomes more disordered without forming a self-screening cell structure due to insufficient strain.. Limitations: The authors state that the strain applied was not sufficient for the formation of a cell-like structure, which typically leads to a decrease in the dislocation outer cut-off radius and Wilkens parameter.. Future work: The authors recommend the mWH method for other researchers studying the structure of deformed HEAs and suggest that the approach can be applied to analyze defects in polycrystalline materials with various crystal structures.. Quote: "Peak profile analysis shows that the dislocation density of the CoCrFeMnNi alloy subjected to axial compression increases with increase in strain and reaches plateau at a strain of 47.5%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can an equimolar-ratio high-entropy design strategy be utilized to overcome the bottleneck of low breakdown strength and poor energy density in dielectric ceramics, specifically within tetragonal tungsten bronze structures?. System: (Sr0.2Ba0.2Pb0.2La0.2Na0.2)Nb2O6 (SBPLNN), a high-entropy tungsten bronze-type relaxor ferroelectric with five equimolar A-site elements (Sr2+, Ba2+, Pb2+, La3+, Na+). Processing: Traditional solid-state method: raw compounds (SrCO3, BaCO3, Pb3O4, La2O3, Na2CO3, Nb2O5) were ball-milled for 4 h, calcined at 1160 °C for 3 h, ball-milled again for 6 h, pressed with 6.5 wt% PVA binder into 13 mm diameter pellets, and sintered at 1220 °C for 3 h. Test conditions: Dielectric properties measured from −120 °C to 200 °C and 10 Hz to 1 MHz; P-E loops and breakdown strength tested up to ~753 kV·cm−1; fatigue tested up to 10^6 cycles at 470 kV·cm−1; temperature stability from −120 °C to 120 °C; frequency stability from 10 Hz to 250 Hz; charge-discharge tested with 300 Ω load resistance. Findings: Achieved a giant recoverable energy density (Wrec) of 11.0 J·cm−3 and a high efficiency (η) of 81.9% under an electric field of ~753 kV·cm−1.; Configurational entropy (ΔSmix) reached 1.61R due to the introduction of five equimolar elements, driving entropy-dominated phase stabilization.; Grain size was refined to an average of ~1.57 μm with an equiaxed feature, contrasting with the anisometric rod grains of typical TTB ceramics.; Dielectric loss was suppressed to ~0.0014 at room temperature and 1 kHz, with a diffuse dielectric peak showing a large ΔT value of 60.5 °C.; Leakage current density was suppressed to ~2.9 × 10-8 A·cm−2 at 50 kV·cm−1, which is 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than other reported compositions.; Demonstrated robust fatigue resistance up to 10^6 cycles with Wrec fluctuating only from 5.51 J·cm−3 to 5.55 J·cm−3.; Achieved an ultra-fast discharge speed with a time to release 90% of energy (t0.9) of 55.8 ns and a power density of 622.21 MW·cm−3.; Atomic-scale analysis confirmed disordered distribution of all five elements in both A1 and A2 sublattices, breaking inherent site selectivity.. Mechanism: The high configuration entropy induces increased atomic-scale compositional heterogeneity and strong non-periodic lattice distortion. The compositional heterogeneity disrupts long-range ferroelectric order, generating ultrasmall polar nanoregions (PNRs) that reduce polarization hysteresis and remnant polarization. Simultaneously, the lattice distortion causes grain refinement, increases resistivity, suppresses leakage current, and enhances electrical homogeneity, which collectively lead to an ultrahigh breakdown strength.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study or the material system.. Future work: The authors propose that the equimolar-ratio element high-entropy strategy is a universal, practical, and efficient method for developing next-generation dielectric materials and highlight the immense potential of tetragonal tungsten bronze-type materials for advanced energy storage applications.. Quote: "realizes a giant recoverable energy density of 11.0 J·cm−3 and a high efficiency of 81.9%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a high-entropy design strategy be utilized to simultaneously achieve ultrahigh recoverable energy storage density (Wrec) and ultrahigh efficiency (η) in lead-free relaxor ferroelectric ceramics?. System: Lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics with the composition [(K0.2Na0.8)0.8Li0.08Ba0.02Bi0.1](Nb0.68Sc0.02Hf0.08Zr0.1Ta0.08Sb0.04)O3 (KNN-H), based on the K0.2Na0.8NbO3 lattice.. Processing: Conventional solid-state reaction method: starting powders were planetary ball-milled for 24 h, dried at 120 °C for 2 h, calcined at 800 °C for 5 h, mixed with 0.5 wt% PVB binder, pressed into pellets at 300 MPa, heated to 550 °C to burn out binder, and sintered at 1230 °C in closed crucibles for 2 h.. Test conditions: Electric fields up to 740 kV cm−1 for P-E loops; temperatures from 25 to 140 °C and frequencies from 1 to 300 Hz for stability tests; cycling up to 10^6 times; charge/discharge tests at 300 kV cm−1.. Findings: A giant recoverable energy storage density (Wrec) of ~10.06 J cm−3 was achieved.; An ultrahigh energy storage efficiency (η) of ~90.8% was realized.; The breakdown electric field (Eb) was enhanced to 740 kV cm−1.; The Vickers hardness (Hv) reached ~7.70 GPa, significantly higher than pure KNN (~3.24 GPa).; The discharge energy density (WD) was ~3.26 J cm−3 with an ultrafast discharge rate (t0.9) of ~34 ns.; The material exhibited temperature-insensitive energy storage (Wrec ~3.38 ± 0.20 J cm−3) from 25 to 140 °C.; The material showed frequency-insensitive properties with Wrec ~4.46 ± 0.25 J cm−3 from 1 to 300 Hz.; Polarization vectors formed polar nanoregions (PNRs) with sizes of ~1–3 nm.. Mechanism: The high-entropy strategy induces 'local polymorphic distortion' characterized by rhombohedral-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic (R-O-T-C) multiphase nanoclusters and random oxygen octahedral tilt. This structure creates a strong random field that reduces PNR size, delays polarization saturation, and drives the system back to a nonpolar state (near-zero Pr), resulting in slim P-E loops, high breakdown strength, and high efficiency.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study itself, though it notes that achieving Wrec ≥10 J cm−3 with η ≥90% simultaneously was a previous bottleneck in lead-free ceramics.. Future work: The authors propose that this high-entropy strategy opens an effective avenue to design dielectric materials with ultrahigh comprehensive energy storage performance to meet the demanding requirements of advanced energy storage applications.. Quote: "A giant Wrec ~10.06 J cm−3 is realized in lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics, especially with an ultrahigh η ~90.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing configuration entropy affect the energy storage performance and domain structure of lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics, and can it enable a breakthrough in energy density and efficiency?. System: (Bi0.5Na0.5)(Ti1-2xFexNbx)O3 (BNTFN-x, x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 1/3) lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics. Processing: Conventional solid-state reaction method; raw materials mixed by planetary mill for 24 h; calcined at 750–800 °C for 5 h; ball milled with PVB binder at 600 r min−1 for 15 h; pressed into 10 mm pellets at ~300 MPa; sintered at 1050–1250 °C for 2 h with sacrificial powders; polished to ~50–80 μm thickness; silver electrodes fired at 550 °C for 20 min. Test conditions: P-E loops at 10 Hz; frequency-dependent loops from 1 to 200 Hz; cycling up to 10^6 times; charge/discharge tests at 16–24 kV mm−1 and 20–160 °C; Weibull distribution analysis with n=10 samples. Findings: Ultrahigh recoverable energy density (Wrec) of ~13.8 J cm−3 and efficiency (η) of ~82.4% achieved in BNTFN-1/3 (ΔSconfig ~1.79R).; Wrec of BNTFN-1/3 achieved nearly 10 times growth compared to low-entropy BNTFN-0 (0.39 J cm−3).; Breakdown field (Eb) increased from 24 kV mm−1 in BNTFN-0 to 64 kV mm−1 in BNTFN-1/3.; Theoretical Eb of BNTFN-1/3 calculated via Weibull distribution is 64.3 kV mm−1 with a Weibull modulus (β) of 28.1.; Nanodomain size decreased from 100–200 nm in BNTFN-0 to ultrasmall PNRs (2–4 nm) in BNTFN-1/3, below PFM resolution.; Average grain size (Ga) decreased from 3.0 μm (BNTFN-0) to 2.2 μm (BNTFN-1/3) with increasing entropy.; Discharge energy density (WD) of ~2.35 J cm−3 and ultrafast discharge time (t0.9) of ~30.4 ns achieved at 24 kV mm−1.; Energy storage performance remained stable over 10^6 cycles with Wrec ~5.88 ± 0.14 J cm−3 and η ~85.5 ± 0.5%.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance enhancement to the enhanced random field and improved breakdown field caused by increasing configuration entropy, which breaks long-range ferroelectric order and decreases nanodomain sizes to ultrasmall polar nanoregions (PNRs). Additionally, the coexistence of in-phase and anti-phase oxygen octahedron tilts creates strong multiple local distortions that delay polarization saturation and increase energy absorption.. Limitations: The text notes that the resolution of PFM was insufficient to effectively identify domain morphology in high-entropy samples, and TEM also could not clearly reveal small-size PNRs, requiring speculation based on HR-TEM Moiré fringes.. Future work: The authors speculate that if the types of elements continue to increase to further improve ΔSconfig, Wrec and η will significantly increase, and they suggest that high-entropy antiferroelectric materials still need to be further designed or attempted.. Quote: "Ultrahigh energy storage density of ~ 13.8 J cm−3 and large efficiency of ~ 82.4% are achieved in high-entropy lead-free relaxor ferroelectrics via high-entropy strategy, realizing nearly ten times growth."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of AlCoCrCuFe high entropy alloy (HEA) particles via friction stir processing affect the wear rate and coefficient of friction of copper surface composites under varying loads, sliding velocities, and sliding distances?. System: Copper matrix reinforced with AlCoCrCuFe HEA particles at 5, 10, and 15 vol%. Processing: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) using a pinless tool for compaction followed by a pin tool rotating at 1000 rpm and traversing at 30 mm/min; groove dimensions: 150 mm length, 5 mm depth, and widths of 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9 mm for respective volume fractions. Test conditions: Pin-on-disc wear tests per ASTM G99 using a 6 mm × 6 mm × 30 mm specimen against an EN31 steel disc (65 HRC) with track radius 30 mm; variables included load, sliding velocity, and sliding distance. Findings: Hardness of the composite reached a maximum of 149 Hv for 15% HEA reinforcement.; The base HEA reinforcement material possessed a hardness of approximately 770HV.; Wear rate decreased dramatically with HEA additions, with the minimum wear loss observed for the 15% HEA-reinforced composite.; Wear rate exhibited a positive correlation with applied load, sliding speed, and sliding distance.; Coefficient of Friction (CoF) increased with HEA addition, showing a negative correlation with wear rate.; Applied load had a severe effect on both wear rate and CoF compared to sliding velocity and sliding distance.; SEM analysis showed deep and wide grooves in unreinforced copper, while damage severity drastically reduced with HEA addition.. Mechanism: The authors attribute improved wear resistance to the high hardness of HEA particles, fine-grain structure from FSP, and the formation of asperities where the soft matrix wears away to expose hard reinforcements that carry the load. Increased CoF is explained by the direct contact of these protruding hard reinforcements with the counterpart and the resistance of harder materials to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The text notes that while wear resistance improves, the introduction of HEA leads to a decrement in tensile properties, and the reduction in wear rate is comparatively smaller for the 15% HEA composite compared to the 10% composite.. Future work: The authors state that the effect of HEA on wear resistance at different sliding conditions has not been explored in detail in previous literature, implying a need for further detailed analysis, though no specific future work is explicitly proposed in the conclusion beyond the current study's scope.. Quote: "Higher hardness values at the level of 770HV were the cornerstone in its selection"

W3172238964.title: Two decades of friction stir processing–a review of advancements in composite fabrication

card: Paper card. Question: To evaluate the feasibility of producing aluminium matrix composites reinforced with different volume fractions of AlCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy particulates using powder metallurgy, and to study the effect of particulate volume on microstructure, mechanical properties, wear response, and corrosion resistance.. System: Aluminium AA-1050 (99.5%) matrix reinforced with AlCrFeMnNi HEA particulates at 1 vol.%, 3 vol.%, and 5 vol.%. Processing: Powder metallurgy route: HEA produced via vacuum arc melting (5 remeltings) and crushed by dry grinding in a planetary mill (10 min work/20 min pause, 4 cycles); powders mixed with methanol, pressed into 14 mm pellets, then sintered in a hot press furnace at 550 °C for 1 h under argon, followed by application of 6500 N load raised at 100 N/min and held for 30 min.. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 1000 nm depth with loads up to 196.13 mN at speeds of 13.3240 mN/s and 2.2207 mN/s with 30 s hold; sliding wear at 10 m/s for 1000 m distance using 100Cr6 steel ball; corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at pH 7 with 10 mV/min scan rate.. Findings: SEM analysis showed reinforcing particle area coverage of 2.04% for 1 vol.%, 4.31% for 3 vol.%, and 7.18% for 5 vol.% composites.; Hardness increased with reinforcement content; the matrix exhibited lower hardness values compared to the HEA particulates (around 57 HRC).; Creep depth of the matrix was considerably higher than the HEA phase, with stress exponent (n) values of 30–35 for the matrix and 58–86 for the HEA.; Wear rates were lowest for samples with increased reinforcement, while the 1% sample showed the highest mass loss in the initial 200 m.; Wear mechanisms included abrasive wear (grooves), oxidative wear (oxide layers), and delamination wear (flake-like debris).; Corrosion curves showed a sustained flat gradient and negative hysteresis loops, indicating susceptibility to localised corrosion controlled by the matrix.; No secondary intermetallic phases or voids were observed at the particle-matrix interface in the 5 vol.% composite.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the increased hardness and wear resistance to the presence of hard HEA particles restricting mass movement and acting as barriers to crack propagation. Creep behavior is explained by dislocation mobility and the complex multi-phase nature of the HEA, where multiple interfaces at lower loading speeds may block dislocations, increasing the required load. Corrosion is driven by galvanic coupling where noble elements (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn) in the HEA particles cause selective dissolution of the Al matrix at the interface.. Limitations: The text states that 'further investigation is required to ascertain' the reversed loading behavior of the HEA reinforcement at lower speeds compared to previous work. Additionally, the corrosion performance was found to be 'not affected by the increasing volume of the reinforcement,' limiting the ability to tune corrosion resistance via volume fraction in this specific system.. Future work: The authors state that 'further investigation is required to ascertain' the reasons behind the reversed loading behavior of the HEA reinforcement at lower speeds, specifically regarding the role of multiple phases and interfacial boundaries.. Quote: "The sintering stage was carried out in the following steps: First, the temperature was raised to 550 °C with a step of 50 °C/min with inert atmosphere using argon gas."

W2742927352.title: Investigations on composites reinforced with HEA particles

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying Ti content (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) affect the phase structure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiTix high entropy alloys fabricated via electro-deoxidization and vacuum hot pressing?. System: CoCrFeNiTix (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) prepared from CoO, Cr2O3, NiO, Fe2O3, and TiO2 oxides. Processing: Electro-deoxidization of mixed oxides in molten CaCl2 at 1173 K pre-electrolysis and 3.1 V for 8 h, followed by Vacuum Hot Pressing Sintering (VHPS) at 1373 K, 35 MPa for 1 h with a heating rate of 30 K/min. Test conditions: Tensile testing at strain rate 10^-4 s^-1; Vickers hardness (150 g load, 70 mm/s); Electrochemical corrosion in 0.5 M H2SO4, 1 M KOH, and 3.5 wt% NaCl with scanning rate 2 mV/s. Findings: Bulk CoCrFeNiTix alloys exhibited a single-phase FCC structure due to high mixing entropy and solid-phase diffusion during synthesis.; Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) increased from 670 MPa (x=0) to 783 MPa (x=1.0) then dropped to 460 MPa (x=1.5).; Hardness increased monotonically with Ti content, ranging from 245 HV (x=0) to 669 HV (x=1.5).; Residual oxygen content in the alloy powders increased proportionally with Ti content due to difficult deoxygenation of TiO2.; Ti addition significantly improved corrosion resistance in 0.5 M H2SO4 by promoting the formation of stable oxide films.; In 3.5 wt% NaCl, Ti0 and Ti0.5 alloys showed higher corrosion and pitting potentials compared to higher Ti alloys.; Ti1.5 alloy exhibited brittle fracture morphology (river pattern) due to secondary TCP phases and stress concentration from residual oxygen.. Mechanism: The FCC solid solution forms due to high entropy and solid-phase diffusion preventing intermetallic segregation. UTS increases initially due to solid solution strengthening and TiC second-phase precipitation, but decreases at high Ti due to residual oxygen forming brittle TCP phases that induce stress concentration. Hardness rises due to lattice distortion from larger Ti atoms and hardening by TiC particles. Corrosion resistance in acid improves via TiO2 film formation, while in NaCl, higher oxygen and secondary phases in high-Ti alloys reduce resistance.. Limitations: The text notes that the molar volume ratio of Ti/TiO2 is small (0.63) making deep deoxygenation difficult, leading to residual oxygen. It also states that carbon deposition from the graphite mold causes Cr7C3 or TiC segregation, and that high Ti content leads to secondary phases that deteriorate corrosion resistance in NaCl.. Future work: The authors state that post-treatment and properties of electrochemically synthesized HEAs have not been sufficiently studied, implying a need for further investigation into post-treatments and optimization of the electrochemical process to reduce oxygen content.. Quote: "The bulk CoCrFeNiTix (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) HEAs could be obtained through vacuum hot pressing sintering process (VHPS), which had a single-phase FCC structure."

card: Paper card. Question: How does doping with different Nb contents (0–9 wt%) affect the microstructure, mechanical properties, and fracture behavior of CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys prepared by high-energy ball milling and discharge plasma sintering?. System: CoCrFeNi-Nbx (x = 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 wt%) high-entropy alloys. Processing: High-energy ball milling (400 rpm, 4 h total with 10 min cooling intervals) followed by discharge plasma sintering (SPS) at 1100 °C, 30 MPa pressure, for 10 min; heating rates: 100 °C/min (0–600 °C), 50 °C/min (600–900 °C), 25 °C/min (900–1100 °C). Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing (cross-sectional area 1.5 mm × 1 mm, tensile rate 0.2 mm/min, original gauge length 5 mm); Vickers hardness (500 g load, 15 s retention); XRD (Cu Kα, 40 kV, 40 mA, 20–90°); SEM/EDS analysis. Findings: Nb0 alloy has FCC single-phase structure with tensile strength 656.3 MPa, yield strength 269.4 MPa, and elongation 62.2%.; Nb9 alloy reaches maximum tensile strength 893.2 MPa and yield strength 775.4 MPa, but elongation drops to 11.8%.; Nb5 alloy shows optimal balance: tensile strength 879.1 MPa, yield strength 491.8 MPa, and elongation 39.8%.; Hardness increases from 201 HV (Nb0) to 336 HV (Nb9), nearly proportional to Laves phase volume fraction.; Laves phase (Co2Nb-type, HCP) forms with Nb addition; its volume fraction increases with Nb content.; FCC matrix is enriched in Co, Cr, Fe, Ni; Laves phase is enriched in Nb (~35%) and depleted in Cr, Fe, Ni.; Fracture mode shifts from ductile (Nb0–Nb5) to brittle (Nb7–Nb9) as Nb content increases.. Mechanism: The large atomic size of Nb causes lattice distortion in the FCC matrix (solid solution strengthening), while the formation of hard, brittle Nb-rich Laves phase provides precipitation strengthening; the trade-off between FCC matrix plasticity and Laves phase brittleness determines overall properties.. Quote: "The results show that with the addition of the Nb element, the lattice distortion of the alloy due to the large size of the Nb atoms causes the microstructure of CoCrFeNi HEAs to change from a single-phase FCC structure to a dual-phase structure of FCC and Laves."
